claims.text: The intervention is to increase the Mo stoichiometric coefficient in the CoCrFeNiMox matrix from x = 0.2 to x = 1.
Increasing Mo from x = 0.2 to x = 1 will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide temperature range.
Increasing Mo intensifies lattice distortion in the FCC phase.
Increasing Mo promotes formation of a hard, Mo-rich tetragonal sigma phase.
Elevated-temperature oxidation and tribochemical reactions produce a continuous, dense oxide/molybdate glaze containing species such as Ag2MoO4.
Additional Mo impedes dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
Mo-induced solid-solution strengthening suppresses plastic deformation and mitigates wear.
The sigma phase provides second-phase strengthening that contributes to reduced wear.
At low temperatures, MoS2 forms a layered, low-shear lubricating film that reduces friction.
Soft Ag reduces adhesive interactions during sliding.
At high temperatures, a layered silver-molybdate-based glaze reduces friction and material removal.
The Mo1 composite will have higher hardness than the Mo0.2 baseline.
The Mo1 composite will have better wear resistance than the Mo0.2 baseline at all tested temperatures.
The coefficient of friction of Mo1 may not be lower than that of Mo0.2 at every low-to-medium test temperature.
The largest friction and wear reductions are expected at 600–800 °C because dense glaze formation dominates in that range.
The Mo0.2 baseline is predominantly an FCC solid solution with minimal sigma phase.
The Mo0.2 baseline has a hardness of 432 HV.
The Mo0.2 baseline has friction coefficients of approximately 0.66 at room temperature, 0.75 at 200 °C, and 0.21 at 800 °C.
The Mo0.2 baseline has wear rates of 13.1 × 10^-6, 98.1 × 10^-6, and 6.6 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m at room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C, respectively.
The proposed effectiveness domain is dry sliding in air against a Si3N4 ball from room temperature to 800 °C at 8 N, 0.15 m/s, and 270 m sliding distance.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis states that Mo1 will reduce both friction and wear over a wide temperature range, while the predicted outcome concedes that friction may not be lower at every low-to-medium temperature. The intended temperature-wide scope is therefore inconsistent.

The hypothesis requires improvement in both friction and wear, but the falsification rule requires joint failure of wear improvement and high-temperature friction/glaze behavior. Consequently, failure of only one required outcome would not necessarily falsify the stated hypothesis.
